title: Why Australia's West Coast Has Only One City
sources: Dutch route, pipeline and wind arrows drawn through main points (approximate)
Coast strip, cyclone coast and Greater Perth: geo/make_regions.py (Natural Earth, buffers; approximate)
Share of WA in Perth, 1911: 'about one third' shown as 33 %

paragraphs.text: Western Australia has nearly thirteen thousand kilometres of mainland coast. Fly along it at night, from the south-west corner to the Kimberley, and almost all of it is dark.

stat.label: Mainland coastline of Western Australia

paragraphs.text: There is one exception. Perth. About eight in every ten Western Australians live in and around that single city. Leave it behind and you can drive for days along the coast and pass only small towns, mining ports and empty beaches.

shots.photo: File:AUS Perth, Central Business District, Kings Park, View 015.jpg

stat.label: Western Australians living in Greater Perth, 2023-24

shots.photo: File:Little yellow caravan on the prairie.JPG
File:Cape Ranges National Park - Flickr - GregTheBusker.jpg

paragraphs.text: But here is the strange part. The other side of Australia is lined with cities. And Carnarvon, on the west coast, sits almost as far from the equator as Brisbane does on the east. Brisbane gets about a thousand millimetres of rain in an average year. Carnarvon gets about two hundred and thirty.

routes.label: Almost the same distance from the equator

shots.photo: File:AUS Brisbane, South Brisbane, Clem Jones Promenade, View 002.jpg

paragraphs.text: Same continent. Nearly the same latitude. More than four times the rain on one side. And now even Perth, the one city that made it, is losing the rain it was built on.

shots.photo: File:Still morning at the Fascine, Carnarvon (cropped).png
File:AUS Perth, Central Business District, Kings Park, View 005.jpg

shots.on_screen_text: Mundaring Weir, in the hills above Perth

paragraphs.text: So why does Australia's west coast have only one city? The answer runs through a wind that blows the wrong way, a river that hides underground, a Dutch shipwreck and a massacre, one of the strongest gusts ever measured on the Australian mainland, a town that was wiped off the map, and a city that now makes its own water from the sea. The first reason is the air itself.

shots.on_screen_text: The dry bed of the Gascoyne

shots.photo: File:Batavia Pl.1 State Library of New South Wales FL3726277.jpg

chapters.title: The Wrong Side of the Wind

paragraphs.text: Reason one. The west coast sits on the wrong side of the wind. Australia lies under a belt of high pressure that circles the globe at about thirty degrees south. Air in that belt sinks, warms and dries out. It is the same belt that makes the Atacama in Chile and the Namib in Africa, two deserts that also sit on the western edge of a continent.

shots.photo: File:A portion of the Atacama Desert along Peru’s southern Pacific coast (iss074e0315662).jpg

paragraphs.text: Around that high pressure, the winds blow from the south-east. On the east coast, those winds come in off the Pacific, loaded with moisture, and hit a long line of mountains. The air rises, cools and drops its rain. That is why Brisbane is green.

shots.photo: File:AUS Brisbane, Central Business District, Brisbane River 007.jpg

paragraphs.text: By the time the same air reaches the west coast, it has crossed thousands of kilometres of dry land. It arrives from the land, not the sea. And there are no high mountains on this side to squeeze out what little moisture is left. The highest peak in the whole state, Mount Meharry, reaches only about twelve hundred and fifty metres, and it sits far inland.

stat.label: Mount Meharry, highest point of Western Australia

paragraphs.text: The ocean should help. Off most desert coasts, like Chile and Namibia, cold water wells up from the deep and keeps the air cool and dry. Off Western Australia, something unusual happens. A warm current, the Leeuwin Current, flows south from the tropics, along the coast. Scientists describe it as the only current of its kind in the world, an eastern boundary current that carries tropical heat towards the pole.

shots.photo: File:Ningaloo Coast and Lake Macleod, Western Australia (MODIS 2021-10-01).jpg

paragraphs.text: The water off this coast is four to six degrees warmer than off other desert coasts at the same latitude. That warmth gives Perth and the south-west their mild, wetter winters. It feeds coral reefs far further south than usual. But it cannot fight the wind. North of Perth, the warm sea sits beside a dry shore.

shots.photo: File:Monkey Mia from the water - panoramio.jpg

stat.label: Sea off Western Australia, against other desert coasts at its latitude

paragraphs.text: Reason two. Without rain, there are no great rivers. The east coast has rivers that run all year. Most rivers in the west run only after a storm, and then vanish.

shots.photo: File:AUS Brisbane, Central Business District, Merivale Bridge 002.jpg

paragraphs.text: The Gascoyne, which reaches the sea at Carnarvon, is the longest river in Western Australia. For most of the year its bed is dry sand. Locals call it the upside-down river, because its water is still there, flowing underneath, in the sand and gravel below the dry bed.

shots.on_screen_text: The Gascoyne reaches the sea at Carnarvon
The dry bed of the Gascoyne
The dry bed of the Gascoyne

paragraphs.text: That hidden water is the only fresh water Carnarvon has. Since about the nineteen twenties, farmers have pumped it to grow bananas, tomatoes and other crops, and Carnarvon became a major supplier of fresh fruit and vegetables for Perth. In the nineteen sixties, so many wells pulled so much water that the groundwater fell, and many of the plantations failed. Since then the state has limited how much anyone can pump.

shots.photo: File:Bathing in the big tank on Perret's plantation, Carnarvon (full).png
shots.on_screen_text: A plantation water tank, Carnarvon, about 1930

stat.label: Limits on pumping after the plantations failed

shots.on_screen_text: The Gascoyne in flood, 2021, from orbit

paragraphs.text: Shark Bay, just south of Carnarvon, shows how harsh this water can be. In a shallow arm of the bay called Hamelin Pool, the sea is about twice as salty as normal. Few of the animals that graze on microbes can live in it. So on its floor, mats of microbes build rocky mounds called stromatolites, the same kind of structures that fossils show on Earth billions of years ago. They survive here because the animals that would eat them cannot. Shark Bay became a World Heritage area in nineteen ninety-one.

stat.label: Salt in Hamelin Pool, against normal seawater
Shark Bay on the World Heritage List

paragraphs.text: One small town, living on one hidden river, under strict limits. That is roughly the most this land can carry without help. And for a long time, the outsiders who saw it decided it could not carry anything at all.

shots.photo: File:Admiralty Chart No 1056 West Coast of Australia. Sheet VIII, Published 1835.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The west coast on an Admiralty chart, 1835

paragraphs.text: Reason three. Europeans found this coast early, and they did not like what they found. The first Europeans known to have landed on the west coast were Dutch. Their ships sailed from the Cape of Good Hope on the strong westerly winds of the Southern Ocean, then turned north towards the spice islands of the East Indies. Turn too late, and you hit Australia.

shots.photo: File:De BATAVIA voor de film onderweg als de NIEUW HOORN (01).jpg

paragraphs.text: In October sixteen sixteen, a Dutch captain named Dirk Hartog did exactly that. He landed on an island at the edge of Shark Bay, nailed a flattened pewter plate to a post, and scratched a record of his visit onto it. It is the oldest European object known from Australia. Then he sailed on. There was no water, no trade and no reason to stay.

shots.photo: File:Drik hartog's plate, 1616 and vlaming's plate, 1697 - cyclopedia of western australia.jpg

stat.label: Hartog's plate: the oldest European object known from Australia

paragraphs.text: Eighty years later, another Dutch captain, Willem de Vlamingh, came looking for a lost ship. On the same island he found Hartog's plate, its post almost rotted away. He put up a new plate in its place and took the old one with him. It ended up in Amsterdam, where it is still on display in the Rijksmuseum. Two visits, eighty years apart, and in between no European had settled anywhere on this coast.

stat.label: Vlamingh replaces Hartog's plate and takes the original

shots.on_screen_text: The coast south of Shark Bay

paragraphs.text: Thirteen years later, the coast showed what it could do to a ship. On the fourth of June sixteen twenty-nine, the Batavia, one of the Dutch East India Company's newest ships, struck a reef in the Houtman Abrolhos, a chain of low islands off today's Geraldton. Most of the people aboard made it onto bare coral islands with almost no fresh water.

shots.photo: File:De BATAVIA voor de film onderweg als de NIEUW HOORN (03).jpg
File:Batavia Pl.1 State Library of New South Wales FL3726277.jpg

paragraphs.text: The commander, Francisco Pelsaert, took a small boat north to the Dutch base in Java for help. While he was gone, a group of mutineers led by a company merchant named Jeronimus Cornelisz took control of the survivors. According to the Western Australian Museum, they killed about a hundred and twenty-five men, women and children. When Pelsaert returned with a rescue ship, the ringleaders were tried and executed on the islands. Almost four hundred years later, archaeologists digging on Beacon Island, where most of the killings happened, are still finding the graves of the victims. Two young mutineers were put ashore on the mainland instead. What happened to them is unknown. The wreck itself was found again in nineteen sixty-three, and part of its hull now stands in the Shipwreck Galleries in Fremantle, a short drive from Perth.

shots.photo: File:Batavia Pl.2 State Library of New South Wales FL3726280.jpg
File:Batavia Pl.5 State Library of New South Wales FL3726286.jpg
File:Batavia Pl.3 State Library of New South Wales M DSM C530.jpg

stat.label: Men, women and children killed by the mutineers

shots.photo: File:Batavia Pl.6 State Library of New South Wales FL3726288.jpg
File:WTF Marlene Oostryck Maritime Museum Batavia from above.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Part of the Batavia's hull, Fremantle

shots.photo: File:WTF Marlene Oostryck Maritime Museum Batavia stern.jpg

paragraphs.text: The English came next. In sixteen eighty-eight, William Dampier landed on the north-west coast. In the account he published in sixteen ninety-seven, he described the soil as dry and sandy, with no water unless you dug wells. His bleak picture of the land stayed the common view for a long time.

shots.photo: File:Schrijver William Dampier in een kleine open prauw op reis naar Aceh (Indonesië), Caspar Luyken, Abraham de Hondt, 1698 - Rijksmuseum.jpg

shots.on_screen_text: Dampier's voyage of 1699, chart by Emanuel Bowen

shots.photo: File:Moll - A map of the world shewing the course of Mr Dampiers voyage round it from 1679 to 1691.png
shots.on_screen_text: Map of Dampier's voyage round the world

shots.photo: File:Low tide at Roebuck Bay, Broome, WA, Australia 01.jpg

paragraphs.text: For more than two hundred years after Hartog, Europeans mapped this coast, wrecked ships on it, and sailed past it. Nobody stayed. When Britain finally did settle Australia, it chose the other side.

shots.photo: File:Admiralty Chart No 1723 The Houtman Rocks, Published 1845.jpg

paragraphs.text: Reason four. When settlers finally came to the west, the land fought them too. In May eighteen twenty-nine, the Swan River Colony was founded where Perth stands today. Its founders had expected rich farmland.

stat.label: The Swan River Colony is founded

shots.photo: File:View of Freemantle (Western Australia) From Church Hill E. of the Town.jpg

paragraphs.text: The soil turned out to be mostly sand. The good farmland was a narrow strip along the banks of the Swan and Canning rivers. Gardens failed. Twenty-one years after it was founded, the colony still had fewer than six thousand settlers.

shots.on_screen_text: The Swan River and the coastal plain

shots.photo: File:Perth, Australia, is split by the Swan River (iss074e0376130).jpg
File:Fremantle, 1832 from original sketch by r morrell - cyclopedia of western australia.jpg

stat.label: Settlers in the colony, 1850

paragraphs.text: What changed things was gold, found far inland in the eighteen nineties. Thousands of miners rushed to Kalgoorlie and Coolgardie, into country with almost no water at all. So the colony did something huge. Its chief engineer, Charles Yelverton O'Connor, planned a steel pipeline to pump water from a dam in the hills near Perth all the way to the goldfields: five hundred and sixty-six kilometres, uphill, with eight pumping stations.

shots.on_screen_text: Pietro Porcelli at work on O'Connor's statue, about 1910

stat.label: Mundaring Weir to Kalgoorlie, eight pumping stations

paragraphs.text: The water arrived in January nineteen-oh-three. O'Connor did not see it. He had taken his own life ten months earlier, after fierce attacks on him and the project in the press. His pipeline still runs today.

shots.photo: File:E37 Clackline Lion Park - Goldfields pipeline.JPG
File:CSIRO ScienceImage 6380 Section of the Perth Kalgoorlie water supply pipeline near Merredin WA 1976.jpg

paragraphs.text: That pipeline shows the pattern of the whole state. Wealth was found far from the coast. And the water to keep people there had to come from Perth. The city became the place everything else depended on.

shots.photo: File:AUS Perth, Central Business District, Kings Park, View 022.jpg

paragraphs.text: And the state kept pulling towards it. In nineteen eleven, about one in three Western Australians lived in Perth. By nineteen forty-seven it was one in two. Today it is eight in ten. Every decade, a larger share of the state moved to the one corner where the rain was reliable.

shots.photo: File:AUS Perth, Central Business District, Kings Park, View 019.jpg

chart.title: People of WA living in Perth
chart.source: Engineers Australia; WA Population Statement 2025 (about one third in 1911)

shots.photo: File:Perth skyline from the Swan River, August 2024.jpg
File:AUS Perth, Central Business District, Kings Park, View 020.jpg

paragraphs.text: Reason five. North of Perth, the coast is not just dry. It is dangerous. According to the Bureau of Meteorology, the north-west coast between Broome and Exmouth is Australia's most cyclone-prone stretch of coastline. Tropical cyclones cross it more often than anywhere else on the continent, mostly between December and April.

stat.label: Cyclone season on the north-west coast

paragraphs.text: In March nineteen ninety-nine, Severe Tropical Cyclone Vance passed close to Exmouth. Just before midday on the twenty-second, the weather office at Learmonth, thirty-five kilometres to the south, recorded a gust of two hundred and sixty-seven kilometres an hour. The Bureau listed it as a record for the Australian mainland.

stat.label: Gust at Learmonth, 22 March 1999
stat.note: Listed by the Bureau as a mainland record

paragraphs.text: Inland, it is the heat. On the Bureau's original records, the Pilbara town of Marble Bar reached at least thirty-seven point eight degrees, a hundred degrees Fahrenheit, on one hundred and sixty days in a row, from the end of October nineteen twenty-three to April nineteen twenty-four.

stat.label: In a row at 37.8 °C or more, Marble Bar, 1923-24

paragraphs.text: The sea itself has killed whole fleets here. In the early twentieth century, Broome, on the north-west coast, was a pearling town, and hundreds of small sailing boats called luggers worked the shallow banks offshore, many crewed by Japanese and Malay divers. In March nineteen thirty-five, a cyclone passed north of the town and caught the fleet at sea near the Lacepede Islands. Twenty-one luggers were lost. About a hundred and forty men drowned.

stat.label: Lost in the cyclone of March 1935
stat.source: Bureau of Meteorology; Federal Cabinet report, April 1935

paragraphs.text: Put those together, a dry coast, cyclones in summer and long runs of extreme heat, and you get a place where building a town is expensive and keeping people in it is harder. Yet some of the richest ground on Earth lies right here.

shots.photo: File:Dusk at Cable Beach, Broome, WA, Australia 01.jpg

paragraphs.text: Reason six. The west coast is rich, but its riches do not need cities. Inland from the cyclone coast lies the Pilbara, with some of the largest iron ore deposits in the world. In the year to June twenty twenty-five, the ports of the Pilbara shipped about seven hundred and thirty million tonnes of iron ore. The state says that is around forty-three percent of the world's seaborne trade in it, and about four fifths of Australia's.

stat.label: Iron ore shipped from Pilbara ports, 2024-25
Of the world's seaborne iron ore trade

shots.photo: File:CSIRO ScienceImage 11678 A Rio Tinto iron ore shiploader in operation in the Pilbara.jpg

paragraphs.text: Most of it leaves through one port. Port Hedland shipped almost five hundred and seventy-eight million tonnes, more than any other bulk export port in Australia. Yet the town around it, including South Hedland, had only about fifteen thousand people at the last census.

stat.label: Iron ore through Port Hedland, 2024-25

shots.photo: File:Admiralty Chart No 1437 Australia - North West coast Port Hedland, Published 1897.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Port Hedland on an Admiralty chart, 1897

stat.label: People in Port Hedland, incl. South Hedland, 2021

paragraphs.text: The reason is simple. Mines here run on huge machines and long trains, not on large crowds of workers. Many workers do not live in the Pilbara at all. They fly in from Perth for a couple of weeks, work long shifts, and fly home. The money is made in the north. The families, the schools and the shops stay in Perth.

shots.photo: File:Mount Newman Mining Co. - panoramio - Seko Naotomo.jpg
File:AUS Perth, Central Business District, Kings Park, View 021.jpg

paragraphs.text: And sometimes a mining town does not just stay small. It disappears. In the gorges of the Pilbara, a town called Wittenoom grew up around a blue asbestos mine. The company closed the mine at the end of nineteen sixty-six, and the government later found the town itself was contaminated.

shots.photo: File:69-07 Centralian Tours 330 Wittenoom Gorge, Australia 1969 (51239610298).jpg

paragraphs.text: The state began winding Wittenoom down in nineteen seventy-eight. In two thousand and six it cut off the power. In two thousand and seven, the town was officially removed from the map. More than two thousand of the roughly twenty thousand people who worked or lived there have since died of asbestos diseases, according to health groups and the state. The last resident left in twenty twenty-two. About three million tonnes of mine waste still lie in the gorge, and the road signs warn visitors to stay away.

stat.label: Wittenoom wound down, its power cut (2006), then removed from the map
Former workers and residents dead of asbestos diseases

paragraphs.text: Reason seven. Even the one city is under pressure, and from the same thing that emptied the rest of the coast: rain. Perth was built on wet winters, carried in from the Indian Ocean by storms from the south-west. The south-west corner is where those winter storms reach the coast most reliably, and that is exactly where the city grew. Its water came from dams in the hills east of the city.

shots.photo: File:AUS Perth, Central Business District, Kings Park, View 007.jpg

paragraphs.text: Since the middle of the nineteen seventies, those winter storms have weakened. According to Perth's water utility, the Water Corporation, rainfall in the dam catchments has dropped by fifteen to twenty percent. But the flow of water into the dams has fallen by about eighty percent, because dry ground soaks up most of the rain before it can run off.

stat.label: Rain in Perth's dam catchments since the mid-1970s
Water flowing into Perth's dams

paragraphs.text: Before nineteen seventy-five, the dams received about four hundred and twenty billion litres a year. In the last decade, the average has been about seventy-five billion. This year, after a dry winter, the utility says little more than twelve and a half billion litres flowed in.

chart.title: Into Perth's dams (billion litres a year)

paragraphs.text: So Perth turned to the sea. It opened its first large desalination plant in two thousand and six, and a second one south of the city later. Together, the plants can now supply about half of Perth's drinking water. The southern plant alone provides, on average, about thirty percent. A third plant, at Alkimos, north of the city, is due to add about fifty billion litres a year from twenty twenty-eight.

stat.label: Of Perth's drinking water made from the sea
From the Southern Seawater plant, on average
A year from the Alkimos plant, from 2028

paragraphs.text: Perth has also been drawing down the water under its feet. In parts of the Gnangara Mound, the great body of groundwater north of the city, levels have fallen by up to ten metres since nineteen eighty. The state estimates about a thousand billion litres of stored water have been lost. So Perth now cleans its own wastewater to drinking standard and pumps it back underground, up to twenty-eight billion litres a year, to refill the aquifers for later.

stat.label: Fall in Gnangara groundwater levels since 1980
Groundwater storage lost
A year recharged into the aquifers

paragraphs.text: Think about what that means. The one city on Australia's west coast now makes a large share of its water from the ocean. The coast's only success story is fighting the same dry wind that kept the rest of the coast empty.

shots.photo: File:AUS Perth, Central Business District, Kings Park, View 002.jpg
File:AUS Perth, Central Business District, Kings Park, View 023.jpg

paragraphs.text: So why does the west coast have only one city? The wind comes from the land, not the sea. The rivers hide underground. The first Europeans who saw this coast sailed on, or wrecked on it. The soil was sand. The north is a cyclone coast. And the wealth that was found could be dug up and shipped out without building towns to hold it.

shots.photo: File:Batavia Pl.4 State Library of New South Wales FL3726284.jpg

paragraphs.text: Perth survived because it had the one corner of mild, wet winters, and then because everything else in the state came to depend on it. Now even that corner is drying.

shots.photo: File:AUS Perth, Central Business District, Kings Park, View 014.jpg
File:AUS Perth, Central Business District, Kings Park, View 009.jpg

paragraphs.text: Some Australians argue the country should build up the north and west, with new ports, new towns and new water. Others say the coast is empty for good reasons, and that the money is better spent where people already live.

shots.photo: File:CSIRO ScienceImage 11678 A Rio Tinto iron ore shiploader in operation in the Pilbara.jpg

paragraphs.text: Whichever way that argument goes, the west coast will keep its shape for a long time. The wind will still come off the land. The rivers will still hide. And the one city on that long, dark coast will keep doing what it has done for almost two hundred years: finding water where the sky will not give it.

shots.photo: File:Dusk at Cable Beach, Broome, WA, Australia 04.jpg
File:AUS Perth, Central Business District, Kings Park, View 022.jpg

paragraphs.text: Should Australia try to build a second big city on its west coast, or leave it as it is? Tell me what you think.

ask.text: A second big city on the west coast, or leave it as it is?

youtube.description: Western Australia has nearly 13,000 km of mainland coast, yet eight in ten Western Australians live in one city, Perth. Carnarvon sits almost as far from the equator as Brisbane and gets less than a quarter of its rain. We follow the answer from orbit: the wind that blows the wrong way, the Leeuwin Current, the upside-down Gascoyne River and Shark Bay's stromatolites, Dirk Hartog's plate and the Batavia massacre, the Swan River Colony and C. Y. O'Connor's pipeline, Cyclone Vance and the Broome pearling fleet, Port Hedland's iron ore and the erased town of Wittenoom, and the city that now makes its water from the sea.
